nameStory: Hindakia gets its name from the Czech phycologist František Hindák, who made important contributions to freshwater algae research. The species name 'tetrachotoma' comes from Greek meaning 'divided into four parts,' referring to how this tiny alga splits into four cells during reproduction.
description: Hindakia tetrachotoma is a microscopic freshwater green alga that you won't see with the naked eye - you'd need a microscope to observe its single-celled beauty. Each cell is incredibly tiny, measuring just a few micrometers across, and appears as a bright green sphere. While individual cells are invisible, large populations can sometimes create a faint greenish tinge in the water. This is a planktonic species, meaning it floats freely in the water column rather than attaching to surfaces.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are only 3-8 micrometers in diameter - far too small to see without magnification of at least 400x

idTips.label: Spherical shape
idTips.description: Cells appear as perfect bright green spheres under the microscope, lacking any obvious surface textures or projections

idTips.label: Four-cell division
idTips.description: During reproduction, cells divide into four smaller cells within the original cell wall, creating a distinctive cross-like pattern

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Cells display an intense emerald green color due to high chlorophyll content, appearing almost jewel-like under proper lighting

idTips.label: Free-floating habit
idTips.description: Unlike many algae, these cells drift freely in the water rather than forming colonies or attaching to surfaces

habitat: Found in clean, nutrient-poor freshwater environments including mountain lakes, pristine ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's higher elevations. Prefers cool, well-oxygenated water with low nitrogen levels, often in areas away from agricultural runoff or urban development. Most commonly discovered in the clearer waters of New Hampshire's White Mountains and Vermont's Green Mountains.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to increase as water temperatures rise and daylight hours lengthen, though still requiring microscopic examination to detect.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when photosynthesis is most active, potentially creating very faint greenish tinges in otherwise clear water.
seasonality.fall: Numbers gradually decline as temperatures drop and light levels decrease, with cells often sinking deeper in the water column.
seasonality.winter: Populations persist at low levels under ice cover, entering a dormant state until spring conditions return.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of lake water can contain thousands of these microscopic green gems, each one photosynthesizing and producing oxygen just like a giant oak tree - they're essentially miniature underwater forests floating all around us!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, Hindakia can be confused with other small spherical green algae like Chlorella species, but Hindakia's distinctive four-way cell division pattern and slightly larger size help distinguish it. Remember: 'Hindakia has four' - the four-cell division is your key identifying feature.
contextualKnowledge: As a member of the Chlorellaceae family, Hindakia is related to Chlorella, which is widely cultivated as a health supplement. However, wild Hindakia species like this one serve as important indicators of water quality - their presence suggests clean, unpolluted aquatic environments.
compareHints: Since Hindakia tetrachotoma is the only Hindakia species documented in New England, compare it with its closest relatives in the Chlorellaceae family like Chlorella species. Hindakia cells are generally larger than Chlorella and show the distinctive four-way division pattern, while Chlorella typically divides differently and has slightly smaller, more uniform cells. The four-part reproductive division is Hindakia's signature calling card.
